clue.text: What one may do on a sunbed: turn sort of orange?

parts.words: What one may do on a sunbed
parts.note: lying on a sunbed is how you brown your skin
a go is a turn, as in a board game

explanation.surface: A sunbed user worries about ending up an unnatural shade of orange.
explanation.walkthrough: Tango is a British brand of orange-flavoured fizzy drink, hence a 'sort of orange'. The surface wants the fake-tan orange; the colon just separates the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Tango is a well-known British fizzy soft drink flavoured with orange, so it is one kind of orange drink.

clue.text: Worked painfully hard to ruin rival date

indicators.note: ruining the given words wrecks their order so the letters are rebuilt another way

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone schemed laboriously to spoil a romantic rival's evening out.
explanation.definitionFit: To travail is an old word for toiling with pain and great effort, so the past tense matches this phrase.

clue.text: Scruffs catch forty winks on beds regularly

parts.note: forty winks is a short sleep

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word it follows, at even steps

parts.note: second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Dishevelled people grab a quick snooze stretched out on beds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scruffs' looks like scruffy people, but it means the backs of necks, as in 'by the scruff of the neck'.
explanation.definitionFit: The scruff is the back of the neck, and the nape is the same part, so the plurals are synonyms.

clue.text: Odd trace of drugs coroner officially documented

indicators.note: odd here means strange or out of order, so the letters are rearranged
a trace is only the slightest hint, so just the opening letter of the word that follows is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A coroner officially notes a strange trace of drugs found at a post-mortem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' looks like it describes the trace, and 'documented' seems a verb for the coroner; in fact 'Odd' shuffles the coroner plus one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on record has been formally noted in an official register, so it is officially documented.

clue.text: Don't worry about the likes of rats, Ned

indicators.note: about suggests the letters are turned around and moved about into a new order

parts.note: rats are classic pests
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone reassures Ned that the rats are nothing to be concerned about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't worry about' reads as one phrase, but 'about' is the anagram signal, applied to the pests plus the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'never mind' tells someone to forget a problem and not be troubled by it, the same as telling them not to worry.

clue.text: New trouble for one that held Jesus' hand?

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A fresh problem arises for a disciple who once held Jesus by the hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like a tender companion; it is the nail of the crucifixion that held his hand to the cross.
explanation.definitionFit: At the crucifixion Jesus' hands were fixed to the cross by metal spikes, so this item literally held his hand.

clue.text: Archdeacon on ecstasy helping with worship

parts.note: an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
a ration is a portion or helping

explanation.surface: A churchman high on ecstasy is lending a hand at the service.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' just places the first piece above the next. Archdeacons in the Church of England carry the title 'the Venerable'.
explanation.definitionFit: Veneration is deep reverence or adoration paid to a god or saint, a near synonym for worship.

clue.text: Drug taker coming up with yours truly? Go on!

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a user takes drugs
yours truly means the speaker, me

explanation.surface: An addict turns up and the speaker is urged to carry on talking.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to continue after a pause, so as an instruction it means carry on or continue.

clue.text: One rambling about politician being on the up and up

indicators.note: about means going around, so the rambling word wraps the politician

parts.note: Roman numeral one
wandering about freely
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A wandering politician seems to be thriving on his travels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rambling' reads as long-winded talk by the politician, but it is the wandering word that wraps him.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on the up and up is getting steadily better, which is what improving means as an adjective.

clue.text: Lament awful, but entertaining head of government

indicators.note: entertaining means hosting or holding something within

parts.note: dire means dreadful

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone complains that something is dreadful yet the prime minister found it amusing.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a slow mournful song for the dead, so it is a musical lament.

clue.text: Slur like individual drinking fifth of tequila

parts.note: as means like

indicators.note: drinking means taking something in, so one word swallows the letter

parts.note: an individual is a person

indicators.note: fifth of means keep only the letter in fifth position of the following word

parts.note: the fifth letter of the spirit's name

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a person for knocking back tequila.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifth letter of tequila is I, not E; it slips between the S and O of PERSON.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast aspersions is to make damaging remarks, so an aspersion is a slur on someone's character.

clue.text: Smashing drink with Harry's granny

parts.note: to sup is to sip or drink
Prince Harry's grandmother was Queen Elizabeth, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys a lovely drink with Prince Harry's grandmother.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword Queen; here she is reached through her grandson Prince Harry.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British words of enthusiastic praise meaning excellent or terrific.

clue.text: In and of itself, a swear word repelled Henry

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: repelled means driven back, so the swear word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a cuss is a curse word
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Henry recoils from someone's profanity.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the cuss is reversed: A, then SSUC, then H.
explanation.definitionFit: 'As such' means considered by its own nature, in the strict sense, which is what 'in and of itself' expresses.

clue.text: Pale yellow wine that's proper going to head

indicators.note: going to head means that word is placed at the front of the other one

parts.note: prim means stiffly correct
rosé is pink wine

explanation.surface: A pale white wine that's respectable enough but still goes to your head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going to head' sounds like getting tipsy; it tells you the proper word sits in front of the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Primrose names the soft light yellow colour of the wild spring flower of the same name.

clue.text: Nothing at all to ask me? Undoubtedly!

definitions.text: Nothing at all to ask me?
definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally not a single query
second meaning: the idiom for certainly

explanation.walkthrough: The first half takes the phrase literally, an absence of queries; the second is its everyday idiomatic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: When something is beyond any query it is certain, so the phrase is an idiom for undoubtedly or certainly.

clue.text: Boorish young drunks spoiled goal and result

indicators.note: spoiled means ruined, so the letters are messed up and reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Drunken football fans ruined the match result after a goal.
explanation.walkthrough: A lager lout is the British term for a young man made rowdy by too much beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager louts are rowdy youths whose bad behaviour comes from heavy beer drinking, matching boorish young drunks.

clue.text: On TV, gales battered a port in Texas

indicators.note: battered means knocked about, so the letters are beaten into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A television report shows storms pounding a harbour on the Texas coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Galveston is a city and seaport on an island on the Gulf of Mexico coast of Texas.

clue.text: Corpse without a head could be little Barney

indicators.note: without a head means losing the first letter of the word

parts.note: a stiff is slang for a dead body

explanation.surface: A headless body might turn out to be a small boy named Barney.
explanation.walkthrough: Barney looks like a name, but a barney is British slang for a noisy quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiff is a minor squabble, so it is a small version of a barney, a row or argument.

clue.text: Likelihood of the morbidly obese avoiding health issues?

definitions.text: Likelihood of the morbidly obese avoiding health issues?

parts.words: Likelihood of the morbidly obese avoiding health issues?
parts.note: surface reading: the odds that a very overweight person stays healthy
setter's reading: an idiom for no chance at all, built on the word for overweight

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, it is the probability for someone heavy; the idiom it points to is a sarcastic way of saying something will never happen.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a sarcastic idiom for very little possibility, and literally names the prospects of a heavy person.

clue.text: Reckon Hoskins is involved in broken tea set

indicators.note: involved in means placed inside, so one piece goes within the other
a broken set is in pieces, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
the setter Hoskins speaking of himself: I am, shortened

explanation.surface: The setter admits responsibility for a smashed tea set.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, so 'Hoskins is' means I'M. TEA SET is shuffled to ESTATE and I'M goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to calculate roughly or judge an amount, which is what reckon means as a verb.

clue.text: Benefit of party member avoiding Green leader

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: avoiding means steering clear of, so that letter is left out

parts.note: a leg is a limb or member

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A political party member keeps away from the Green Party's leader for some advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party member' reads as a politician, but it splits into a party and a limb. The dole is the British name for state unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: The dole is the informal British term for state unemployment money, a welfare benefit.

clue.text: Brilliant hidden …

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for amazing or terrific

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue but is only for the surface; this clue is complete on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is dated slang for marvellous, and literally means beyond view, so it fits both words.

clue.text: New Milan university could produce these

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for the answer; read with the whole clue it means the graduates a university turns out

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh version, so the letters are made into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A newly founded university in Milan will turn out graduates.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only 'these', but the whole clue frames it: what a new university could produce are graduates.
explanation.definitionFit: Alumni are former students and graduates, the people an institution of learning turns out.

clue.text: … clue? Heard composer's a visionary

parts.note: as in 'I haven't a clue', meaning no notion

indicators.note: heard means we want the sound of the composer's name, not its spelling

parts.note: the Hungarian composer Franz Liszt

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, someone hears that a composer is a dreamer.
explanation.definitionFit: An idealist pursues lofty ideals and imagines how things could be, so is a visionary.

clue.text: Is it not common to have sex after the pub?

parts.note: an inn is a pub
it is slang for sex

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it is normal to sleep with somebody after a night at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places the slang word for sex behind the pub. 'Common' marks the answer as slang: innit is a British street contraction of isn't it.
explanation.definitionFit: Innit is a vulgar or casual British contraction of 'isn't it', so it is a common way of saying 'is it not'.

clue.text: Complete course of Nordic language (spoken)

indicators.note: spoken means the word is said out loud, and its sound is used

parts.note: the language of Finland

explanation.surface: Someone completes a course in a Scandinavian language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course of' is a loose link here, as if 'Complete' is a matter of how the language sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To finish something is to bring it to an end, so as a verb it means complete.

clue.text: One little business on a Mediterranean island

parts.note: Roman numeral one
biz is a short form of business
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone runs a small company on a sunny holiday island.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza is one of Spain's Balearic Islands, in the western part of that sea, famed for nightlife.

clue.text: Money? Tons is kept beneath throne room

indicators.note: in a down entry, beneath means one word sits below the other

parts.note: the throne is jokey slang for the toilet, so its room is the toilet
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: A huge stash of cash is hidden under a monarch's throne room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throne room' sounds royal, but the throne is slang for a toilet; loo is the British informal word for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Loot is informal slang for money, as well as meaning stolen goods or plunder.

clue.text: Part of an insect found in casino tumbler

indicators.note: found in means the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A bug is spotted in a whisky glass at the casino.
explanation.definitionFit: The notum is the plate on the back of an insect's thorax, a section of its body.

clue.text: Withdrawal is over? Uplifting feeling to be drug-free!

indicators.note: drug-free means without the drug letter, so that letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
elation is great happiness
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: An addict celebrates having come off drugs and finished withdrawal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdrawal' and 'drug-free' suggest rehab, but withdrawal is the definition and the drug is just E, dropped from the feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolation is a state of being cut off from others, and withdrawal is retreat from company.

clue.text: One strung out in a court before judges?

definitions.text: One strung out in a court before judges?

parts.words: One strung out in a court before judges?
parts.note: surface reading: an addicted defendant appearing in a court of law
setter's reading: a mesh stretched across a sports court with umpires watching

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strung out' suggests a drugged defendant and 'court before judges' a trial; the court is for a racket sport and the judges are line judges.
explanation.definitionFit: The mesh across the middle of a lawn or hard court is stretched taut with cord, and line judges officiate around it.

clue.text: Skirt of the First Lady that Bill puts on

indicators.note: putting something on means wearing it, so one word is clothed by the other

parts.note: Eve was the first woman in Genesis
an ad is an advertisement, a bill

explanation.surface: A president named Bill puts on his wife's skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' and 'Bill' point to the Clintons; the lady is the first woman in the Bible and the bill is a poster.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt something is to go round its edge rather than through it, the same as evading it.
